statements.body: The climbing gym currently uses paper liability waivers for all members and visitors.
The front desk queue at peak times is a significant operational problem.
The gym's insurer conducts annual audits that include review of signed waivers.
The gym's lawyer has stated that signed paper originals are the legally required form of record.
The gym wants to offer digital waiver signing at a kiosk and in advance of arrival.
The project will target a climbing gym context with a front-desk check-in workflow.
Digital signatures will satisfy the gym's insurer and legal counsel as equivalent to wet signatures, but this has not been confirmed by either party.
Whether the gym's lawyer and insurer will accept digitally signed waivers as legally sufficient replacements for paper originals.
What waiver content, versioning, or audit-trail requirements the insurer's annual audit actually mandates.
Whether 'going fully paperless and shredding everything' is a goal for this phase or a future aspiration contingent on legal and insurance sign-off.
The decision to stop printing and shredding paper originals is deferred until legal and insurance acceptance of digital records is confirmed.

concerns.coverage: Peak-time front desk queues caused by paper waiver signing are the immediate operational pain; the gym also carries indefinite paper storage burden. Both exist today without this project.

Front desk staff are the primary operators. Gym members and walk-in visitors are the signatories. Gym management, the insurer, and legal counsel are stakeholders whose requirements constrain the solution.
Waivers currently enter as paper at the front desk. The desired future state allows signing at a kiosk or before arrival. Exit point and audit handoff process are not yet described.
Signed waiver records must currently be retained indefinitely per legal counsel. The shape, volume, and export format required for annual insurer audits are unknown.

Liability waivers are legally significant documents; an invalid or lost digital record could expose the gym to uninsured liability. The lawyer's current position treats paper originals as the only legally safe form.
Legal counsel requires signed paper originals to be kept; this is a hard constraint until explicitly overturned by legal and insurance sign-off. Indefinite retention is mandated.
Going fully paperless and shredding existing paper records is explicitly not a goal for the current phase; it is contingent on legal and insurance acceptance and is deferred.
No observable success criteria have been stated. Reduced peak-time queue length and insurer audit pass rate are implied but not defined by the user.

candidates.body: When a member signs digitally at the kiosk or in advance, how will a signed paper original be produced and retained so the lawyer's paper-originals requirement is still satisfied in this phase?
candidates.whySelected: The ledger simultaneously commits to digital signing (82783c05) and a hard constraint that signed paper originals are the legal record (09e0b16e, ba255155), with paperless explicitly deferred (0a2b88b9). The first slice cannot be designed until we know whether digital signatures get printed, countersigned, batch-printed nightly, or something else — this is the single biggest unresolved shape of the workflow.

candidates.body: What would the front desk staff observe at peak time that would make you say the digital waiver system worked — for example, a target check-in time per visitor or queue length?
candidates.whySelected: Success coverage explicitly states no observable criteria exist (77c6d09a). A concrete peak-time target bounds how ambitious the first slice must be and gives an acceptance test.

candidates.body: During the insurer's annual audit, how are waivers currently pulled and reviewed — what does the auditor actually ask to see?
candidates.whySelected: The data coverage (e5daa934) marks the audit export format and handoff as unknown (7eb942a0). Knowing what auditors inspect determines what the digital system must record and export, but it bounds the slice less directly than the hybrid workflow question.

contradictions.summary: The gym wants signing to happen digitally at a kiosk or in advance, but the ratified constraint says signed paper originals are the legally required record and the decision to stop paper is deferred; the ledger does not say how a digital signature becomes a paper original in the interim.

readyAdvice.why: All core concerns have coverage, but the digital-signing-versus-paper-originals tension leaves the first slice's workflow shape undefined, and success has no observable criteria. Resolving the hybrid workflow question is the minimum needed before a slice can proceed.

statements.body: When a new climber signs digitally at the kiosk or via an advance link, the front desk sees a green check indicator on that member's profile at check-in.
Audit retrieval will be performed by searching signed waiver records by member name and date range.

Whether the digital workflow described (kiosk or advance link → green check on profile → searchable audit records) still produces a signed paper original, or whether the lawyer's paper-originals requirement is being silently dropped without explicit sign-off.
What system or role is responsible for managing the member profile that displays the green check indicator, and whether one already exists or must be built.

concerns.coverage: New climbers sign digitally at a kiosk or via an advance link; front desk sees a green check on the member profile as confirmation; audit retrieval is by name and date range. How paper originals are produced within this flow remains unresolved.
Signed records must be searchable by member name and date range for audit purposes. Whether this search is performed by front desk staff, management, or the insurer directly is not stated.
A green check visible on the member profile at check-in is implied as the operational success signal for the front desk workflow, but no quantitative queue or audit targets have been stated.

candidates.body: Does the gym already have a member management system with individual profiles that the green-check indicator can attach to, or must member profiles be built as part of this project?
candidates.whySelected: The approved workflow depends entirely on a member profile showing a green check at check-in, and the ledger explicitly records as unknown whether such a system exists. Whether this is an integration or a build-from-scratch changes the first slice's scope more than any other open question, so answering it bounds the slice most directly.

candidates.body: What specific records, formats, or evidence does the insurer's annual audit require you to produce when they review signed waivers?
candidates.whySelected: The audit is a hard external checkpoint and the ledger records its actual requirements as unknown. Knowing what the auditor inspects determines what the digital system must capture and export from day one, but it constrains the data model more than the first slice's boundaries.

candidates.body: What observable change would tell you the project worked — for example, a target reduction in peak-time queue length or check-in time per climber?
candidates.whySelected: Success coverage explicitly notes no quantitative criteria have been stated; the green check is an operational signal, not evidence the queue problem is solved. A concrete target lets the first slice be judged, though it does not change what gets built.

readyAdvice.why: The workflow, constraints, and paper-originals handling are well framed, but the slice cannot be scoped until you know whether a member profile system exists to host the green-check indicator, and success has no measurable target yet.
